#4391. Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day

Eating mango and avocado every day could offer unexpected benefits for heart health, according to new research. In a study lasting just eight weeks, adults with prediabetes who regularly ate both fruits experienced improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, without gaining weight or consuming more calories.

The findings could be especially relevant to the one in three (98 million) Americans with prediabetes, a condition in which blood sugar levels are elevated but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, the research suggests that incorporating these two nutrient-rich fruits into everyday meals may help support cardiovascular health.

Researchers at Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) investigated the effects of an Avocado-Mango (AM) diet that included one medium Hass avocado and one cup of fresh mango each day. Participants followed this eating plan for eight weeks, while a comparison group consumed a similar diet in which the fruits were replaced with carbohydrate-based foods containing equivalent calories.

The results revealed notable differences between the groups, particularly in how well their blood vessels functioned and how their blood pressure changed over time.

One of the clearest improvements involved the ability of blood vessels to expand as blood flows through them. This flexibility helps maintain healthy circulation and is an important indicator of cardiovascular health.

To evaluate this response, researchers measured flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a commonly used test of endothelial function (blood vessel health). The endothelium is the thin layer of cells lining the inside of blood vessels, where it helps regulate circulation and the widening and narrowing of arteries.

Among participants eating avocado and mango, the measurement increased significantly to 6.7%. In contrast, it declined to 4.6% in the control group. The difference suggests that regularly consuming these fruits may help blood vessels function more effectively.

Blood pressure measurements also showed encouraging changes, especially among male participants. Men in the control group experienced an average increase of 5 points (mmHg) in central blood pressure, while those consuming avocado and mango saw a reduction of approximately 1.9 points.

Diastolic blood pressure, the lower number in a blood pressure reading, reflects the pressure inside arteries when the heart relaxes between beats. Maintaining healthy levels is important because elevated blood pressure can place additional strain on the cardiovascular system. Researchers noted that the differences observed in the study could be clinically meaningful if they persist over time.

Importantly, the cardiovascular improvements occurred without significant changes in participants' body weight or total calorie consumption. This suggests that the nutritional quality of the foods people eat may influence heart health even when their weight remains stable.

“This research reinforces the power of food-first strategies to help reduce cardiovascular disease risk, particularly in vulnerable populations like those with prediabetes,” said Britt Burton-Freeman, PhD, Principal Investigator and Professor at Illinois Tech. “It’s an encouraging message: small, nutrient-dense additions—like incorporating avocado and mango into meals and snacks—may support heart health without the need for strict rules or major dietary overhauls.”

Beyond the improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, participants eating mango and avocado consumed more fiber, vitamin C, and monounsaturated fat. These nutrients are associated with cardiovascular wellness and may help explain some of the observed benefits.

Researchers also identified improvements in certain indicators of kidney health, including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a measurement used to assess how effectively the kidneys filter waste from the blood.

However, the fruits did not produce significant improvements in every health measurement. Cholesterol levels, blood sugar, and markers of inflammation remained largely unchanged compared with the control group.

Together, the results suggest that regularly including nutrient-rich fruits in the diet could be a practical way to support cardiovascular health, particularly for people with prediabetes who face an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Although mango and avocado have very different flavors and nutritional profiles, they provide complementary nutrients that support several aspects of cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Mango provides dietary fiber (2g/serving, 7% DV, Mango serving size: ¾ cup) and is an excellent source of vitamin C (50% DV). Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from damage, while fiber contributes to healthy digestion and may help with blood sugar regulation, weight management, and cardiovascular wellness.

Avocado offers another combination of potentially beneficial nutrients. It contains fiber (3g/serving, 11% DV, Avocado serving size: 50 g (1/3 of a medium avocado)), which plays a role in managing cholesterol, blood sugar, and body weight.

It also supplies unsaturated fats (6g unsaturated fats), which can support heart health by helping reduce LDL cholesterol, often called bad cholesterol, when they replace less healthy fats in the diet. Additionally, avocado contains potassium (250mg, 6% DV), a mineral involved in regulating blood pressure.

By providing fiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and potassium, mango and avocado offer a convenient way to increase the nutritional value of everyday meals. However, the study did not establish whether eating the two fruits together provides greater benefits than consuming either fruit separately.

Incorporating these fruits into meals does not require a complicated eating plan. Their contrasting flavors and textures make them useful ingredients in salads, smoothies, and grain bowls.

For example, fresh mango can add sweetness to a savory dish, while avocado contributes a rich, creamy texture. Both can be used in recipes such as Mango Avocado Tuna Ceviche or an Avocado and Mango Topper.

Additional recipes and nutritional information are available at Mango.org and LoveOneToday.com.

The investigation included 82 adults between the ages of 25 and 60 who had prediabetes and were classified as having overweight or obesity (BMI 25–35 kg/m2). All participants were generally healthy, did not smoke, were not following specialized diets, and had no major chronic medical conditions.

Over eight weeks, participants followed calorie-controlled eating plans modeled on typical American dietary patterns. One group ate a medium Hass avocado and a cup of fresh mango daily, while the control group received carbohydrate-based alternatives with comparable calorie content.

To make the comparison as consistent as possible, researchers prepared and supplied meals covering 75% of each participant's estimated daily calorie needs. Participants chose their remaining foods independently, allowing some flexibility while helping the researchers limit differences between the two diets and encourage adherence.

The primary measurement was flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a noninvasive method for assessing how effectively blood vessels respond to increased circulation. Researchers also examined blood pressure, blood sugar, and other metabolic indicators, inflammation, kidney function, and dietary nutrient intake.

Despite the additional fruits, the avocado and mango group did not experience significant changes in body weight or overall calorie intake. This finding suggests that incorporating nutrient-dense foods into an otherwise balanced diet may improve certain aspects of cardiometabolic health without necessarily contributing to weight gain.

The study had several strengths, including its carefully controlled feeding approach, two parallel comparison groups, and emphasis on whole fruits rather than isolated nutrients or supplements.

However, researchers also acknowledged important limitations. The intervention lasted only eight weeks, so it remains unclear whether the improvements would persist over months or years. The participants also represented a relatively narrow population of adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity, meaning the findings may not apply equally to people with different health conditions or dietary habits.

The research measured cardiovascular risk indicators rather than long-term outcomes such as heart attacks or strokes. Larger and longer studies will be needed to determine whether the observed changes translate into lasting reductions in cardiovascular disease risk.

Nevertheless, the findings offer an encouraging indication that relatively modest changes in food choices may benefit blood vessel health, even without weight loss or a major dietary overhaul.

This study was supported through an unrestricted grant from the National Mango Board (NMB) and the Hass Avocado Board (HAB). NMB and HAB had no role in the study design or findings.

#4389. NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover breaks historic record after traveling 28 miles

NASA's Perseverance rover has reached an impressive new milestone, traveling farther across another world than any vehicle before it. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), the rover's total driving distance reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), establishing a new record for travel on another celestial body. The achievement was even recognized by Guinness World Records, which presented a commemorative plaque to Perseverance's engineering twin on Earth.

The rover had actually come close to breaking the record about two months earlier. On Sol 1947, Perseverance was just 200 meters short of the milestone, a distance it could have covered in a single trip using its Autonomous Navigation (AutoNav) system.

But reaching the record was not the team's immediate priority. Perseverance was exploring an area filled with scientifically valuable ancient rock formations, so it spent weeks making short trips between locations to examine exposed rock surfaces. These investigations included grinding away thin layers of rock and conducting detailed measurements up close. Once the scientific work was complete, the rover resumed its journey and soon surpassed the previous distance record.

"Two months ago, (Perseverance) sat about 200 meters away from the milestone, a distance easily achievable with a single drive... However, the rover found itself in a very scientifically interesting area and spent time (investigating) ancient rock outcrops. When Perseverance was finally ready to move on to a new site, it sailed past the record."

How NASA Improved Perseverance's Driving Capabilities

Covering more than 28 miles on Mars has required Perseverance to overcome difficult terrain while testing new approaches to robotic driving. Its journeys through tightly packed boulder fields and across steep hillsides have given NASA engineers valuable experience, helping them improve the rover's ability to navigate hazardous landscapes.

To expand what Perseverance can safely handle, engineers conducted thousands of computer simulations and adjusted several operating limits. The rover can now tolerate tilts of up to 24 degrees, while the minimum clearance beneath its protective belly pan has been reduced to 20 centimeters (about 7.9 inches).

The team also introduced several important improvements to the driving system. Updated braking software helps the rover avoid collisions with rocks, and the electrical current limits for its steering motors have been nearly doubled. Engineers also added "dynamic slip tables" to its flight software, allowing the rover to better anticipate how much its wheels might slip on different surfaces.

Another technique involves driving across slopes in ways that help keep the wheels securely positioned on exposed bedrock. Together, these changes allow Perseverance to handle challenging terrain more effectively as it continues exploring Mars.

A Mars Rover That Can Navigate Without GPS

Among the rover's most significant technological advances is a system called onboard Global Localization (GBLC). This technology gives Perseverance a way to determine its position on Mars without relying on directions from Earth.

The system uses a powerful commercial processor originally installed in the Ingenuity Helicopter Base Station. By comparing images captured from the Martian surface with pictures taken from orbit, it can calculate the rover's location in global coordinates after completing a drive (as though we had GPS on a world without it).

Knowing its position independently is a major advantage. It allows Perseverance to cover greater distances without needing people on Earth to repeatedly determine its location, potentially making future exploration faster and more efficient.

However, this approach introduced an engineering challenge. Unlike the rover's main flight computer, the additional processor was not specifically designed to withstand the intense radiation conditions on Mars. The planet has a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field, leaving electronics exposed to radiation that can interfere with their operation.

In particular, radiation can cause "transient bit flips" that unexpectedly change information stored in computer memory, potentially disrupting software. To address this problem, engineers developed software protections that help the processor operate reliably despite the harsh environment.

The Next Frontier in Autonomous Mars Exploration

NASA is also investigating how generative AI could make the rover even more independent. As missions involve longer journeys and increasingly complex operations, the team wants to reduce the time and resources needed to plan safe routes.

The technology could help generate driving plans for the many individual segments of a longer journey, providing guidance that Perseverance's AutoNav system can use to navigate the terrain.

After traveling 45 kilometers (more than 28 miles), Perseverance has already provided engineers with extensive experience in navigating the Martian landscape. Those lessons are now shaping new technologies that could transform how robotic explorers operate on distant worlds.

And the journey is far from over. As Perseverance continues climbing higher along the rim of its Martian crater, NASA is preparing for the next major advances in autonomous exploration.

Materials provided by NASA. Original written by Vandi Verma, Chief Engineer for Robotic Operations at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4388. 10 RPGs That Are Unexpected Masterpieces

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Thanks to the diversity with which the genre can be expressed, role-playing video games constitute a large part of my favorite experiences in the interactive medium, as they encompass a practically unparalleled plethora of possibilities.

Both an isometric horror title and a first-person medieval fantasy can be RPGs, giving all players, regardless of their tastes, the opportunity to find tailor-made masterpieces within the genre.

Of course, being among the most popular categories in the entire industry, finding an adventure curated to suit our tastes is no easy task, as it's common to need dozens of hours to fully enjoy each of its journeys.

Therefore, in order to save you many afternoons and with the aim of appealing to as many gaming interests as possible, I invite you to read this list of ten RPGs that are unexpected masterpieces.

If you like Paper Mario, you already know exactly what Bug Fables: The Everlasting Sapling has to offer, though I say this as one of the highest compliments I can give.

It's a game with very traditional foundations but an execution brimming with personality, offering a compelling world and story that truly keeps you engaged, especially due to its unique theme.

However, its greatest marvel lies in its gameplay. From exploration to turn-based combat combinations, side quests, bosses, and customization, the overall mechanics work flawlessly, captivating both newcomers and veterans of this type of game.

This independently created gem from Panama deserves all the recognition it can get. Rest assured, Bug Fables: The Everlasting Sapling is such an outstanding work that, at times, I think it surpasses its main inspiration.

Speaking of surpassing your muses, I've read many discussions about Path of Exile already surpassing Diablo, and frankly, comparing the most recent performance of both franchises, I find it difficult to argue otherwise.

Although they have different approaches, it's undeniable that Grinding Gear Games' creation, both the original and its sequel, has reached such levels of content density and attention to detail that they ceased to be "a clone" many years ago.

Instead, we're talking about one of the greatest representatives of the isometric RPG genre, with a consistently captivating experience that puts your job at risk because, once it hooks you, it only lets go after several hundred hours.

Imagining in 2013 that Path of Exile could go head-to-head with its category's benchmarks seemed impossible, but today, what's truly unbelievable is calling it anything less than a masterpiece of its kind.

Since the end of the last decade, efforts to find a true successor to Disco Elysium have tripled year after year, but even so, I couldn't have anticipated that a game like Esoteric Ebb would be its true spiritual heir.

Although it boasts enough distinctions to stand on its own merits, it's clear that the foundation was laid by the 2019 marvel, which allowed Christoffer Bodegård to craft an outstanding adventure from the dialogue to the worldbuilding and immersion.

Each narrative path is more captivating than the last, and even without voice acting, which forces you to read for hours on end, the cadence and rhythm between exploration and conversations, both internal and with others, are measured with truly commendable precision.

If you're a fan of Disco Elysium or Dungeons & Dragons, Esoteric Ebb strikes a perfect balance that, I can say with complete certainty, no other title this decade has even come close to achieving.

If you're looking for a 16-bit adventure, these SEGA Genesis RPGs are a great place to start.

A decade and a half ago, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim's release sparked a subsequent odyssey to become the next great medieval first-person RPG, and I believe that title finally belongs to Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avalon.

The mere comparison is the highest honor that can be bestowed upon this wonderful dark fantasy, which nevertheless knows perfectly well how to distinguish itself from Bethesda's icy landscapes without losing an ounce of immersion.

Moreover, the title manages to compensate for its idol's weaknesses by including choices that truly feel meaningful, as well as a much more fluid and demanding combat system that not only increases the challenge but also the reward of leveling up and becoming gradually more skilled.

Considering the remarkable post-launch support that its developers provided for free, Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avalon is a blessing for the genre that deserves to be rewarded with a chance.

Dread Delusion looks further back than the 2011 Game of the Year and draws its inspiration from two superb titles, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind and King's Field, and the result is as outstanding as you'd expect from that combination.

Its distinctive aesthetic, blending a feverish PlayStation 1 dream with a lush color palette, immediately captivates the eye, yet the experience truly enchants for hours thanks to the sheer satisfaction of getting lost in its picturesque settings.

That said, you need a very high tolerance for its combat, as it lacks depth and isn't particularly rewarding. Rather, it's a necessary sacrifice to immerse yourself in its splendid world, which is worth every second.

It's a tougher recommendation, especially in modern times, given how much better it feels when you're not using your weapons, but make no mistake: Dread Delusion is one of those titles that, if it's right for you, will win you over thoroughly.

There are certain video games whose ultimate goal is to hook you for hundreds of hours without you even realizing it or being able to stop, and Grim Dawn is undoubtedly one of them.

I went in expecting to find a good RPG and little else, and ended up finding a lifelong companion that I would spend countless afternoons with, mainly due to its absurdly deep and satisfying replayability.

The art is superb, the music is tremendous, the story and atmosphere stand out, the creativity with which it allows you to experiment with builds is impressive... It has everything you could expect from an ARPG, and even more.

For how magnificent it is, I'm afraid Grim Dawn isn't talked about enough, and precisely for this reason, you wouldn't expect that behind it lies one of the most magnificent isometric role-playing games ever made.

There are still numerous RPG gems to enjoy before the year ends.

Appearances in the video game industry are easily deceiving because the essence lies in interaction. This allows a pixel art game like Look Outside to appear harmless, while beneath the surface, it's a masterpiece of cosmic horror.

However, despite its themes inducing fear through impressively disturbing designs, it's a turn-based RPG where your decisions shape both the party and the story, which quickly spirals into madness.

Despite its modest origins in RPG Maker, the game compensates for its technical limitations with outstanding art and writing, aided by a functional gameplay component that ensures the campaign flows smoothly, so the protagonist—the atmosphere—never suffers in the slightest.

Look Outside is among the finest indie games of the last couple of years, although it seems the community hasn't quite grasped the greatness with which it represents the work of H.P. Lovecraft... Yet.

We all know that everything Obsidian touches turns to gold, though for reasons that are hard to understand, the gaming community seems to have overlooked this when it came to Alpha Protocol.

Yes, the action sequences are decent at best, and technically speaking, it's a subpar product, but the stealth, writing, and decision-making are so magnificent that I struggle to imagine a world where the negative outweighs the positive.

You can experience the story multiple times in diametrically opposed ways and have campaigns that feel unique, with memorable characters, plot points that truly make you think, and a worldbuilding that lures you to explore every last detail.

Since I know there are two types of RPG fans, one who prioritizes gameplay and another who prioritizes narrative, I must emphasize that only the latter will truly enjoy Alpha Protocol, though their lives will be completely changed once they play it.

From Mass Effect 2 to Elden Ring, these RPGs make putting off the main quest worthwhile—and sometimes even essential to the outcome.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance was a very pleasant surprise, but it appealed to a limited niche due to the specificity of its medieval setting. Therefore, I don't think any of us expected Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 to become the new gold standard for RPGs.

All future titles of this genre that prioritize immersion and the complexity of their systems will have to look to Warhorse Studios' masterpiece, which demands a titanic yet worthy effort to show why it's one of the finest works the genre has produced this decade.

By polishing absolutely everything from its predecessor and improving upon it as much as humanly possible, it's a perfect sequel that doesn't fall short in any area, being extraordinary in its narrative, gameplay, interactivity, audiovisuals, and even its overall atmosphere.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is the blueprint that every first-person RPG should take into consideration for years to come, which is an astounding affirmation to say considering that the original was just very good.

Over the years, I've made it my mission to champion Dragon's Dogma as the most underrated video game of the century, and unfortunately, not even the sequel's success has allowed me to hang up my gloves in that endeavor.

Capcom has numerous masterpieces to its name, though this one in particular stands out for how far ahead of its contemporaries it was at its release, offering an epic fantasy scope barely explored by a couple of other titles within the genre in all its history.

The scale at which Gransys allows us to develop a heroic tale against colossal and captivating beasts is breathtaking, compelling you to lose yourself in a classic mythology that enchants you from its goblins to its dragons.

Thanks to the spectacular gameplay and customization options, where skirmishes are remarkably large and visually stunning regardless of the class you choose, it's a title that could hardly have been anticipated, especially considering what its competitors were doing at the time.

Years go by, and Dragon's Dogma keeps aging like the finest wine, waiting for the video game industry to finally recognize it as one of the past decade's generational titles.

#4387. Extra weight may be aging your brain faster than you think

Carrying excess weight may affect more than physical health. New research from the University of Georgia suggests that having a higher body mass index may also speed up cognitive decline, potentially causing memory and thinking abilities to deteriorate more quickly with age.

Some cognitive changes are a natural part of getting older. Remembering information, thinking clearly, and processing new details can become more difficult over time. For healthy adults, however, these changes are usually relatively mild and develop gradually.

The new findings suggest that excess body weight may accelerate this process. Researchers found that people with higher body mass index (BMI) experienced faster declines in memory, overall cognitive performance, and executive functioning. These abilities are essential for everyday activities such as concentrating, planning, organizing tasks, and regulating emotions.

To investigate the connection, the research team analyzed data from a nationally representative study that tracked more than 8,200 adults over age 50 for 24 years.

Higher BMI Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline

The results revealed a consistent relationship between body weight and cognitive health. Each one-point increase in BMI was associated with a faster rate of cognitive decline, suggesting that even relatively small differences in body weight could matter over time.

The association was strongest at the eighth year of the study, and adults older than 65 showed the most pronounced effects.

Despite the concerning findings, researchers also identified a potentially encouraging opportunity to protect brain health. Managing body weight may help slow cognitive decline, with possible benefits becoming apparent within just two years.

"We found that if people managed their weight, they could significantly lower their rate of cognitive decline in just two years," said Suhang Song, the study's lead author and an assistant professor at the University of Georgia's College of Public Health. "That makes BMI one of the most easily modifiable risk factors when it comes to aging well."

How Excess Weight May Affect the Aging Brain

Obesity, generally defined as a BMI of 30 or higher, has been associated with poorer brain health. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly why carrying excess body weight may interfere with memory and other cognitive abilities.

Several biological processes could help explain the connection. Excess weight may promote inflammation, impair blood circulation, and contribute to insulin resistance. Together, these changes could increase the likelihood of cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, and other forms of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant given how widespread obesity has become in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately two in five Americans meet the criteria for obesity when BMI is used as the sole measure.

Some scientists argue that BMI alone does not provide a complete picture of obesity. They support a broader definition that also considers waist measurements and medical conditions associated with excess weight. Using those additional criteria, the estimated proportion of Americans classified as having obesity rises to 75%.

Weight Management Could Help Protect Brain Health

The potential connection between obesity and cognitive decline is especially concerning as dementia becomes increasingly common. More than 7 million Americans currently live with dementia, and researchers expect that number to double by 2050.

Although the study does not establish that excess weight directly causes cognitive decline, its findings highlight body weight as a potentially important factor in maintaining cognitive health. Because weight can be managed, researchers believe it could offer an opportunity to reduce the risk of worsening memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.

"There are no cures for dementia," Song said, "which is why it is critical to identify and address any modifiable risk factors we can find to prevent it."

The research was published in the Journal of Neurology. Coauthors from the University of Georgia College of Public Health include Meng Hsuan Sung, Zhuo Chen, Janani Rajbhandari, Grace Bagwell Adams, Mahmud Khan, Ye Shen, and Xiao Song. Qianhui Xu and Xia Song also contributed to the study.

#4386. 6 JRPGs to Play If You Loved Final Fantasy Resonance

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

Final Fantasy Resonance is here, and it is already earning high praise from critics and players alike. Boasting an overwhelmingly positive score on Steam, the JRPG has been showered with acclaim for its combat systems, its compelling cast, and its triumphant return to Final Fantasy roots, serving as a love letter to fans of the franchise's 90s golden era.

If you cherished everything Rain and Lasswell's title brought to the table and want more, I have put together a list of other JRPGs to dive into if you enjoyed Final Fantasy Resonance. We have titles featuring modular Job systems, gorgeous pixel art, and secret-packed worlds that will extend your playtime far beyond the main story. It has never been a better time to be a JRPG fan.

Final Fantasy Resonance traces its lineage back to Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, and like many mobile gacha projects, it wears its mainline references and influences proudly. You know who else excels at wearing their JRPG influences on their sleeve? Indie developers. And speaking of phenomenal indie JRPGs, Chained Echoes is a masterclass. If you haven't played it yet, fix that immediately.

First off, Chained Echoes doesn't feature a traditional class system, so if that is your primary draw, the other entries on this list might suit you better. However, if you are looking for stunning pixel art, a gripping narrative, lovable characters, and a nostalgic trip down memory lane, whether through familiar tropes of yesteryear or simply the authentic feel of a 16-bit classic, you owe it to yourself to try Chained Echoes. Its turn-based combat loop is iconic, progression feels clean yet engaging, and its world exploration stands among the finest in the genre. It is thoroughly worth your time.

Plenty of hidden gems in the mobile world deserve a second chance.

Live A Live is delightfully unorthodox, and neither its combat layout nor its narrative structure shares much common ground with Final Fantasy Resonance. Their primary shared trait is the HD-2D visual engine. You might ask why I am recommending it here, and the answer comes down to character focus. Final Fantasy Resonance shines through its incredible cast, successfully translating gacha origins into a complete offline adventure by turning side characters into quest givers and granting them a well-deserved spotlight.

This often-overlooked SNES classic is entirely character-driven. At the start of the journey, you select from several distinct scenarios, each featuring its own protagonist, narrative arc, and setting. The structure feels episodic, but everything weaves together brilliantly by the end. Final Fantasy Resonance places that same heavy emphasis on its cast, so if character development was your favorite aspect, Live A Live will deliver in spades.

Fantasian might be one of the most underrated JRPGs on the market. Developed by Mistwalker under the direction of Hironobu Sakaguchi, the creator of Final Fantasy, Fantasian deserves far more mainstream recognition. Granted, the game originally debuted on a limited platform with Apple Arcade (where I first played it), but the release of Fantasian Neo Dimension brought it to consoles and PC, and you should definitely give it a shot.

Comparatively, the main parallel it shares with Final Fantasy Resonance is its turn-based foundation, though even the combat has its own distinct flavor. Fantasian introduces a unique trajectory targeting system where abilities feature varied area-of-effect paths. Each character follows their own skill tree, and while offering roughly three distinct build directions per party member, it lacks the deep modular customization of Resonance. Still, that comforting sense of playing a classic JRPG from a bygone era, bringing warmth to your heart as you revisit retro design sensibilities, is undisputed. If you want pure nostalgia, Fantasian is the way to go.

Our reviewer earned a platinum trophy and gave Final Fantasy Resonance a 10/10. Check out DualShockers' review of Final Fantasy Resonance.

One of my favorite parts of watching new players jump into Final Fantasy Resonance was seeing them unlock fresh Visions and map out synergy builds for their party. I could practically see the gears turning as they calculated which abilities would mesh best with each character. If that customization loop was your favorite part of the experience, I highly recommend picking up Bravely Default.

Any entry in the series will do, but both Bravely Default II and Bravely Default Flying Fairy HD Remaster will scratch that build-crafting itch (I personally find the second half of the original game a bit tedious, hence my primary recommendation for Bravely Default II). The Job system functions almost identically to Visions in Final Fantasy Resonance: the more you level up your Jobs, the wider your build options and combat potential become. Who knows, you might just discover your next favorite Bartz-style combo in Bravely Default.

If Final Fantasy Resonance left you feeling nostalgic, it is only fitting to revisit the pinnacle of pixel remaster releases. This is doubly true if you have yet to play Final Fantasy VI, as you will recognize countless references while discovering why so many fans rank the sixth entry as the franchise's absolute peak. Final Fantasy VI is simultaneously accessible and deeply complex across all of its design layers.

The combat uses the classic Active Time Battle system, but each party member has unique innate strengths that can be further customized through Espers. The story avoids focusing on a single protagonist, instead distributing screen time across an ensemble cast to build a living, captivating world. During the game's second half, the path forward is left entirely in your hands. Ultimately, you will get to experience one of the true masterpieces of the JRPG genre, or reconnect with it if you have not checked out the Pixel Remaster edition yet.

Final Fantasy Resonance proves that classic Final Fantasy ideas still work, from turn-based combat and jobs to overworld exploration and dungeons.

The most obvious choice on this list is Octopath Traveler II. While I still suggest playing the original first to avoid getting too comfortable with the sequel's refinements, nothing stops you from diving straight into the second title. Octopath Traveler II takes the foundation established by Square Enix's inaugural HD-2D release and elevates every aspect, from storytelling and combat mechanics to visual polish.

Octopath Traveler II previously held the highest review score for an HD-2D title before Final Fantasy Resonance arrived, which speaks volumes about both games' quality. Both titles offer unmatched character customization, with the Visions in Final Fantasy Resonance mirroring the flexibility, dynamism, and build variety found in Octopath Traveler II's Job system. It offers more HD-2D charm, more heart, and endless fun

#4385. Arc Raiders just keeps breaking its own Steam player records

Word of mouth has done wonders for the popularity of Arc Raiders, clearly more than all the pre-launch marketing and hype.

Arc Raiders just cannot be stopped. The extraction shooter from Embark Studios has once again attracted more players over the weekend than it has in its launch week, and over its first weekend on the market.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

The day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

That figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

To everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside new Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. And, if you just jumped in over the weekend, you’re definitely going to find these Arc Raiders tips very helpful.

#4384. Eternal Anima Hands-On Preview – Strive How I Want To

Eternal Anima is the time-twisting RPG revealed during the big September Nintendo Direct that looked like a Square Enix HD-2D game but isn’t. It is also the game with the “Never Strive For A Better Tomorrow” splash screen. After playing the game for roughly an hour within developer Marvelous Inc.’s Tokyo office, I eschew that line – I will, in fact, strive for a better tomorrow, if only so I can play more Eternal Anima one day.

The world has essentially come to its final act in Eternal Anima. Urvis Ael is the last remaining bastion of civilization in a flooded world. That said, living in Urvis Ael isn’t all that bad; just don’t strive for a better tomorrow or really any kind of change. Protagonist Wade breaks those rules and sets out on an adventure, feeling deep down that a better life is possible.

Wade is bestowed with the power of Psychometry, which lets him look into the past, view memories, and inherit abilities and classes for use in combat. My hands-on time with Eternal Anima is mostly focused on combat, and for good reason: it rules. It is turn-based combat, but with a time-turning twist. Wade also has the power of Future Sight, which means he already knows exactly what every enemy will do each turn, reflected in the UI. Every ability has an action speed shown on the timeline at the bottom of the screen. You can always see an enemy’s upcoming action, who they will target, and even the outcome.

Combat in Eternal Anima is less about hitting enemies harder and more about hitting them smarter. When you attack an enemy's weaknesses with Wade or other party members, you knock them back on the battle timeline, pushing their predecided actions back in the move queue. Your goal is to push them back enough that you kill them before they can attack, or, for bigger enemies, knock them off the timeline in what’s known as a Break. This cancels their action, opening up your party for another round of attacks.

The battle system doesn’t feel as active as a standard turn-based RPG; instead, it makes you feel more like a god playing with action figures. You decide what happens, then sit back and watch it all unfold.

Everything is depicted in a beautiful, bokeh-enhanced art style that’s unique to Eternal Anima, despite the initial HD-2D impression. I love how the world and enemies look, which makes it even more disappointing that the characters are rendered as chibi. It doesn’t gel with the game’s painterly visuals and clashes with its heavier thematic tones.

As I explore Eternal Anima’s miniature settings, which resemble closed-off dioramas placed carefully on a larger world map, I take part in fishing minigames, collect items, defeat enemies, and encounter NPCs from the past, like Fletcher. After I interact with a glowing sword on the ground, an animated flashback plays, detailing Fletcher’s story and ending with a notification that I received a bow from his past.

As I continue through this world, some two centuries before my time, I encounter a man from this period who’s trying to save his forest hometown from flooding. Of course, I already know this will happen in my timeline because the entire world is flooded, but Wade suspects that if he can convince this person of the looming threat, he can change the present by altering the past. My demo ends shortly after, but now, a month removed from the preview, I’m still thinking about Eternal Anima, specifically its combat.

A lot of turn-based combat makes you feel powerful. But Eternal Anima’s makes you feel like a genius, and that’s smart and novel. I’m left striving for March now.

#4383. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

#4382. Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation

For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.

Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.

The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.

Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.

Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.

In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.

"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."

A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines

The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.

The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.

One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.

Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.

This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.

Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.

Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.

However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.

Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.

A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure

The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.

The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."

For the more than one billion people living with hypertension, this shift in thinking could have significant implications. Instead of concentrating almost exclusively on reducing salt, future dietary recommendations may increasingly emphasize the combined benefits of consuming less sodium and more potassium.

The underlying message is straightforward: better blood pressure control may depend not only on what people remove from their diets, but also on what they add.

Materials provided by University of Vermont. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4380. 10 Legendary Weapons You Should Have in Borderlands 4

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

Borderlands 4 has a lot of legendary weapons. With the first entire year of content for the game being done, there are now over 160 different legendary weapons that you can choose from.

This only covers the actual weapons, like legendary assault rifles and shotguns, and not the grenades, shields, and class mods you can get. When choosing a weapon, there is a lot to consider.

At this point, there are several weapons that you should have in your bank or on your character that have stayed consistently strong. If you don’t have these weapons, you should probably start farming for them in case there are future DLC plans.

Crow-Sourced is not a legendary weapon, but I am counting it anyone because it is a Pearlescent and they are more rare than legendary items in Borderlands 4. This weapon is one of the Pearlescent weapons added with the first DLC titled Mad Ellie and the Vault of the Damned.

To obtain this assault rifle, you need to make your way over to the Captain Willis boss fight in The Maelstrom. In other words, you won’t get it until the end of the DLC, but it is well worth the wait.

This weapon has the Left of the Murder ability, which makes it fire out random projectiles as you shoot it. Charging the weapon increases the number of projectiles, making it more lethal the more it is charged.

Captain Willis will give you a run for your money in the Mad Ellie and the Vault of the Damned DLC for Borderlands 4.

The Swan Song is one of those weapons that you can use to clear a room very quickly, which means it is a guarantee that you should have it on your characters. This weapon fires fast, hits hard, and even shoots cannonballs.

That’s right, you read that correctly, it first cannonballs. Thanks to its Cannonball ability, you can shoot out cannonballs from the underbarrel of this weapon. Each kill with this weapon grants additional cannonballs, with four being the maximum.

As a weapon, the Swan Song is very powerful, but the underbarrel packs a massive punch, so it is important to continuously use it as you take down enemies. Speaking of takedowns, you get this weapon from the Takedown at Hadron Abyss.

The Darkbeast is one of my go-to weapons when I create a new character. I have a level 30 version of this weapon for new characters, and I always make sure to get one at max level as well for each character.

This SMG packs a serious punch, with it often outperforming other weapons that I use on my characters. Its Parley ability makes it so bullets pierce enemies, and have a 5% chance to cause an explosion when they hit an enemy.

Thanks to this weapon's amazing fire rate, that 5% seems to proc very often, causing major damage. You will never be let down by the Darkbeast, and you can get it from Voraxis in the Coastal Bonescape.

With how I mentioned that the Darkbeast tends to outperform other weapons, there are some that still outperform it, and the Ohm I got is one of them. This is an electric legendary SMG that fires a laser at opponents, and it will absolutely destroy shields.

It has the ability Energy Transfer, which boosts its damage by 50% whenever your shield is active. However, it consumes your shield in the process. This can be prevented if you have an overshield, so any character can get massive damage with this weapon if they just have an overshield.

The best part about this ability, besides the damage, is that it doesn’t consume ammo when you have a shield either, allowing it to fire infinitely until your shield is gone. You can get this weapon from the second Ripper Queen fight.

If you want a weapon that can delete a boss’s health bar, look no further than the Hot Slugger. A few shots from this can annihilate a health bar if you have the right build.

This legendary shotgun has the Blazing Barrel ability, which gives it a 30% damage boost for 10 seconds after you get a kill. This can stack up to three times for a massive 90% damage boost if you keep getting kills.

You can stack this damage during a boss fight by killing minions and then destroy the boss’s health bar. There are multiple builds that can take advantage of this weapon, and it is amazing.

The Convergence has been around since the start of Borderlands 4 and it still stands as one of the best legendary shotguns in the game, and it is one that you can get relatively easily. It is also a gun that can carry you through many hardships.

This weapon has the Asymptotic ability, which it doesn’t give an explanation for, but you can easily tell what it does as soon as you fire the weapon. Every time you hit an enemy, additional shots converge onto that enemy dealing additional damage.

This causes the weapon to deal some massive damage to enemies. Combined with its fast fire rate, you can easily wipe out health bars in no time. This weapon is dropped from Bramblesong in the Bittervein Augur Mine.

There are many bosses in Borderlands 4, but only Bramblesong has the Convergence as a dedicated drop.

Don’t you just wish that your guns had triple the bullets that you could embed into the bodies of your enemies? Well, the Triplicate, one of the best DLC weapons, aims to deliver, as it will indeed fill your enemies full of lead.

This weapon has the Tripled ability, which makes it so additional explosive projectiles get lobbed whenever you hit an enemy. This makes the weapon overpowered, and capable of taking down groups of enemies in record time.

If you manage to get a shotgun alternate fire mode on this weapon, it will score multiple hits, allowing multiple projectiles to spawn out of the enemy, and when used against larger enemies, it is a death sentence. You can get this weapon from The Reject Prototype in the Amara and the Vile Shadow DLC.

The Golden God is amazing as long as you don’t mind continuously buying ammo for it, as it will use a ton of ammo. However, that ammo loss is okay since you will annihilate every enemy you look at.

The ability Rage make it so that the Golden Gun does not break when you hit the heat threshold. Instead, it continuously consumes greater and greater amounts of ammo until you eventually run out.

This allows you to continuously output damage at an impressive rate, but you will just use a ton of ammo in the process. This weapon can be obtained by farming Idolator Sol, which is one of the earlier bosses in the game.

Stray is a legendary sniper rifle that was available from the get-go when Borderlands 4 launched. All you needed to do was make your way over to the Tendercage Ripper Drill Site and kill the boss called Pango Bango.

Pango Bango drops three weapons, but Stray is by far the best of them. This legendary sniper rifle has the ability stray, which makes it fire two secondary bullets that home in on nearby targets.

This makes it great for clearing out crowds, and one of the best sniper rifles in the game. It is a weapon, like the others on this list, that works very well with most builds, and can be utilized by any of the characters effortlessly.

At this point, everyone should have the Bod in either their bank or on their character, as this weapon is fantastic, and is amazing for testing out builds. The reason is that is counts as every type of weapon.

The All-Arounder ability on it makes it so that it counts as a shotgun, assault rifle, sniper rifle, pistol, and SMG. This also means that it is affected by every type of damage increase, even for specific weapon types.

Even more, the damage bonuses can stack, meaning you can get the benefit of skills that increase damage for SMGs and shotguns on this weapon. To obtain the Bod, you will want to farm Axemaul in Carcadia Burn district of Dominion.

#4379. Arc Raiders has proven that extraction shooters can be popular, with over 4 million copies sold in under two weeks

Arc Raiders has sold even more copies, which we should've guessed, given that the game keeps breaking its own concurrent player records.

It’s pretty clear at this stage that Arc Raiders is one of the biggest launches of 2025. More interesting than the numbers themselves, however, is that this is an extraction shooter - a subgenre which has typically been thought of as niche.

If you’ve been paying the PvPvE game any attention, you could easily see how (and why) it keeps breaking its own records.

Today, publisher Nexon announced in a press release (via Gematsu) that Arc Raiders has now sold over 4 million copies. The game came out on October 30, which means it managed to sell that many copies in a little over 10 days.

The news comes on the same day that developer Embark Studios announced that the game had more than 700,000 concurrent players across all platforms over the weekend. Over the same weekend on Steam alone, Arc Raiders broke its own Steam concurrent record with a new peak of 462,488 players - which is a significant chunk of that 700,000+ player base.

This marks the second time the extraction shooter has broken its own concurrent player records, which is something very few games have managed in the past. Arc Raiders remains a top-seller, too. On Steam, it’s currently the second-best seller globally (by revenue), sitting just below Counter-Strike 2.

“The many different ways you play and participate in ARC Raiders have completely blown us away, going far beyond what we ever imagined. You surprise us, you outsmart us, and you keep us on our toes. We wouldn’t have it any other way,” the developer wrote on Twitter.

Embark recently published a roadmap to highlight all the new content coming to the game over the remainder of this year. The first new map is set to arrive this month alongside new Arc units, new gameplay items, new events and more.

Just over the weekend, the game received several new Map Conditions that completely alter the way they play. The developer has already rolled out a couple of updates since launch, in order to tackle exploits and fix a few launchday bugs.

If you’re currently hooked on this gem of a game, we guarantee that our Arc Raiders gameplay tips will have at least one you didn’t know about. We also have more guides on how to find some of the more elusive items in the game, such as olives, lemons and apricots, and prickly pears.

#4376. Arc Raiders' new map will be unlocked through a community event that starts today, and everyone has to donate

It looks like it's going to take the Arc Raiders community a bit of work to unlock the game's next map.

As many of Arc Raiders’ regular players predicted, the game’s first post-launch map won’t just be available for everyone, it will instead be closely tied to a community event. Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

The event kicks off today alongside the release of the game’s latest patch. The ask is relatively simple: players must commit Basic Materials to the project so that the tunnels can be rebuilt. This option will be available to anyone who’s played at least five rounds.

If you’ve spent any time in Arc Raiders, you’ll know that Basic Materials are things like Metal parts, Fabric, Chemicals, Rubber Parts, and Plastic Parts - most of which are easy to find in the game’s various maps.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the new map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a new progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

Developer Embark describes the new environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the new map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The update will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap update will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

In case you’re still missing them, here’s how to find lemons and apricots, prickly pear, and olives.

#4375. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 16, 2026

Welcome to spooky month where lawns suddenly grow giant skeletons, it's cold enough for a hoodie, the remakes of Resident Evil 2, 3, and 4 released on Switch 2, and we're all prepping to hunker down for Winter. And Grand Theft Auto VI.

We're still in the thick of new release season which, fun fact, used to just be the month of November. But now it starts in August and ends in March, give or take a few weeks.

Before we get to our regularly scheduled weekend recommendations, though, here are some of the biggest Game Informer stories of the week.

It has been a long wait for a brand new Castlevania game, and frankly, I think Belmont's Curse has been worth the time spent in the queue. Charles Harte agrees, as he wrote in his review, "Belmont's Curse is a strong reminder of why the Castlevania series is so influential, with a rich world, tense combat, and a map chock-full of secrets. While this latest entry certainly pays homage to the Castlevanias of yore, it also breathes fresh life into the franchise, making me excited for its future. Castlevania is back, and between Rose Belmont and Evil Empire, it's in great hands."

The game comes from the team behind Dead Cells, a game heavily influenced by Castlevania to begin with, and the result shows how great a fit the team and franchise is. Controlling Rose Belmont feels great, the world is big and fun to explore without being overbearing, and beating each boss is a rewarding challenge. I often feel one mark of a good game for me is if it keeps me up past my bedtime, and Belmont's Curse is, unfortunately, doing a great job of making me feel tired all day. But that's a good thing.

The short pitch for Silver Pines is that it is a Metroid-inspired game crossed with a Silent Hill game. That's a good hook on its own, but what makes it stand out (at least in the limited time I have so far spent with it), is its animation. I don't know that it was actually rotoscoped (think the original 1989 Prince of Persia), but it feels like it was, which makes it look great and lends it an intentional level of uncanny valley that aids the creepy atmosphere. Throw in a dash of Twin Peaks energy, and you end up with something that feels unique against a sea of comparable (but often well-designed) Metroid-inspired games.

Just Dance is an frequent tradition in my household. We don't play it every year, but I was eager to check out Decades of Hits because of its included soundtrack. Just Dance generally leans on contemporary music and as a dad facing down his forties (who is still very cool, right? Right?!) I appreciate the chance to learn about recent pop hits and make a fool of myself in front of my family, but I like how musically diverse this entry is.

You have Sabrina Carpenter, Chappell Roan, and Olivia Rodrigo songs (which I adore), but you also get ABBA, Spice Girls, No Doubt, Daft Punk, Britney Spears, Sum 41, TLC, Gorillaz, Run DMC, Billy Joel, and Elton John among many others.

Also, in recent years, Just Dance has started its own tradition of including at least one shockingly impressive stop-motion animated sequence. I am not sure what executive at Ubisoft is accidentally approving the budget for the continued creation of these types of videos, but I hope they never notice because they're great.

You really can’t go wrong with any Jackbox game. Sure, there are some occasional duds in the packages, but there are always at least one or two super fun games that are always worth returning to. 12 is out this week and includes a game about sorting trivia questions into the right categories at high speed, one where you try to make the most ridiculous greeting card, a game encouraging silly debates, one that identifies connections among everyone playing, and finally Hyperface, where you manipulate selfies.

After an earlier release on VR platforms, the rhythm game Maestro recently made its way onto Switch and Switch 2, including a physical game cartridge launch. If you've always secretly loved the idea of stepping up onto the podium for a try at the conductor's gig, it's one worth tracking down. The game includes a number of classical hits from the likes of Beethoven, Vivaldi, and Tchaikovsky, but there's also the chance to play more contemporary tracks like those you'd hear in Star Wars or Game of Thrones. With Joy-Cons in hand, you'll keep the tempo, cue in musicians, adjust dynamics, and more. The accompanying visuals and "storytelling" aren't going to blow your mind, but the included music is hard to beat, and with occasional exceptions where the game misread my motions, I found the motion-tracking mostly up to the task of nailing the fantasy.

If you spent hours playing the early Toy Story games, then the retro compilation masters at Digital Eclipse have something for you in the form of Toy Story: Retro Roundup. On top of Toy Story, Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue, Toy Story 2, Buzz Lightyear of Star Command, and Toy Story Racer (including multiple versions of many of these), you can also get your hands on the 1998 A Bug's Life game. It may not have the breadth of extra content of something like Digital Eclipse's Atari 50 or Tetris Forever, but it's a fun stroll down memory lane with some behind-the-scenes interviews and materials. Alongside this retro collection, there's also the separate Toy Story 3 Complete Edition, also released by Digital Eclipse this week.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I~III] – yes, that’s really what it’s called – is out on Nintendo Switch 2, and after spending some time with it, man, it feels right at home on the console. This collection includes Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 +2.5 ReMix (which itself includes a bunch of Kingdom Hearts games, including 1 and 2), Kingdom Hearts HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, and Kingdom Hearts III + Re Mind DLC. Basically, it has everything you need to catch up on the Kingdom Hearts saga before Kingdom Hearts IV launches next year.

As for actually playing these games, they feel amazing on Switch 2, courtesy of HD resolutions, on handheld and docked, and 60 FPS gameplay. I don’t know why exactly, but playing the Kingdom Hearts series on Switch 2 just feels right. It probably has something to do with just how many of these games were Nintendo console originals. Nonetheless, if you’re new to Kingdom Hearts or looking for a new place to tear up while "Dearly Beloved" plays, this Switch 2 collection will satisfy your needs.

This new standalone version of Forest Shuffle does more than transplant the theming into the Smoky Mountains of North America. It has also allowed its creators to refine balance, add new elements (like an intriguing new water/river terrain), create a more vibrant and visually beautiful presentation, and overall, up the value and playability of the game across the board. In short, it's what I think is the best version of an already very good game.

For newcomers, the Forest Shuffle formula is a card game that involves a mix of card hand management and tableau-building, as you slowly play out a forest scene onto the table, filled with unique trees, animals, and plants, and gathering points for the types and variety of things living in your woods. It's an approachable and visually enchanting game that still offers plenty of strategic depth as you plan out the shape and potential of your nature scene, all while planning against the impending arrival of winter.

#4374. Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta

Scientists are still working to understand why autism develops. Genetics are known to play a major role, but researchers have also found that conditions during pregnancy can influence the likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.

A new study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) has uncovered a surprising connection between inflammation during pregnancy, changes in the placenta, and the development of autism-like traits in male mice. The findings suggest that certain developmental disruptions may begin much earlier than previously recognized, potentially offering new clues about autism's origins.

"To truly understand autism spectrum disorder, we have to look beyond the brain," CSHL Associate Professor Lucas Cheadle says. "Our work suggests that maternal immune activation and changes within the placenta are a gateway to autism for some unique individuals."

Scientists Identify an Early Window of Vulnerability

To investigate how inflammation affects fetal development, Cheadle and his colleagues triggered an immune response in pregnant mice at different stages of pregnancy. They used a substance that mimics the immune system's reaction to a viral infection without actually introducing a virus.

The researchers discovered that mouse fetuses were especially vulnerable when inflammation occurred 12.5 days into pregnancy. According to Irene Sanchez Martin, a postdoctoral researcher in Cheadle's laboratory, approximately one-third of the fetuses showed developmental abnormalities within just 24 hours.

Scientists have investigated the effects of maternal immune activation for decades, but these findings reveal signs of developmental disruption earlier than researchers had previously observed.

Even more striking was the difference between male and female fetuses. Across every experiment, autism-like traits appeared only in males, while females continued developing normally.

This unexpected distinction could provide insight into why autism is diagnosed substantially more often in boys than girls. What makes the finding especially intriguing is how early the difference appeared, before many of the biological changes normally associated with sex-specific development.

"It's really fascinating, because we're looking at an age which precedes hormonal surges. It precedes sexual differentiation in the brain and many other regions. So, it's surprising there would be a sex-based difference this early."

A Surprising Connection Between the Placenta and Autism

To determine why some developing mice were affected while others appeared protected, Cheadle and Sanchez Martin examined the placenta, the organ that connects a developing fetus to its mother and supports its growth throughout pregnancy.

Their attention centered on specialized cells called spongiotrophoblasts, which occupy a region of the mouse placenta where maternal and fetal cells interact.

In fetuses that developed normally, this part of the placenta remained healthy. However, male fetuses showing developmental abnormalities also had visible damage to these specialized cells.

Spongiotrophoblasts play an important role in helping the mother's immune system tolerate the developing fetus. This protection is essential because the fetus carries genetic material from both parents and is not genetically identical to the mother.

The researchers found that maternal immune activation could interfere with this protective function. When these placental cells become damaged, the mother's immune response may begin affecting the developing fetus in harmful ways.

Why Female Fetuses May Have a Hidden Advantage

The findings raise another intriguing question: Why were male fetuses vulnerable while females appeared unaffected?

One possibility is that male embryos produce distinctive proteins that can trigger an unfavorable maternal immune response following a viral infection. Another explanation is that female embryos possess some form of protection that helps them withstand inflammation during this sensitive developmental period.

Cheadle says, "A protective mechanism may exist within the female that could be harnessed to help the male. We're trying to understand how autism emerges in both sexes," he explains. "The evidence says that there are potentially different mechanisms."

These possibilities suggest that biological pathways involved in autism-like development may differ between males and females. Understanding those differences could help researchers identify why some individuals are more vulnerable to certain environmental influences during pregnancy.

Cheadle's team plans to investigate both male and female mice more closely to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these contrasting responses. Their work could eventually identify new targets for treatments and lead to strategies for intervening earlier in developmental processes associated with autism.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and do not establish that the same mechanisms cause autism in humans, they highlight an unexpected possibility: Important clues to autism's earliest development may lie not only in the brain, but also in the placenta and its interactions with the maternal immune system.

Materials provided by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
