#4256. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4255. Review: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered

Godzilla fans are eating well. At the time of writing, we are on the brink of a new Toho release, a direct sequel to Goji’s first Oscar-nominated film, Minus One. There's also the next entry in Legendary's MonsterVerse to sate fans of the Western arm of the franchise (even though they have been a little Kong-heavy of late). Now, Tokusatsu mayhem is coming back to consoles, as original developer Pipeworks and Atari revamp their 2002 GameCube classic Destroy All Monsters. It smashes its way onto Switch 2 with Unreal Engine 5 visuals, online multiplayer, and some nice quality-of-life bonuses.

Destroy All Monsters Melee is a 3D arena fighter where you can choose from 12 iconic (well, maybe not Orga) kaiju and duke it out in major cities across the globe. It's an absolute joy to play for fans of the franchise, and it's accessible enough that anyone can jump in and relish the city-trampling mayhem.

There is a thin wraparound story that, while patently ridiculous, is in keeping with the lunacy of the series' Japanese entries. An alien race called the Vortaak has invaded Earth, unleashed the inhabitants of Monster Island and taken control of the kaiju that come pouring out. You play as the one friendly monster that has to battle their way to the alien mothership and take on the Vortaak's cybernetic facsimile of Earth's mightiest monster - Mechagodzilla.

That's the overarching plot, and there's only a tiny sliver of story across a couple of cinematics in the game's Adventure Mode, so don't expect a rich narrative. This game is mostly monster fights, and in this respect, it does not disappoint.

There really isn't much more to be said about the joyous spectacle of hefting Gigan over your head and hurling him into the side of a skyscraper. You can fill Anguiris with a faceful of atomic breath or fly rings around your opponent as Rodan. Destroy All Monsters Melee is filled with these moments of wonder amidst what is a fairly straightforward brawler. There are no elaborate combos here, no precise hitboxes, and no need for frame counting. There’s just multiple building-sized animals wailing on each other.

Each monster has basic punch and kick combos, coupled with powerful variants triggered by a push of the right stick. A power move knocks enemies flying at the cost of speed (Godzilla's tail whip is overpowered on any difficulty), while projectile abilities help manage distance.

Monsters can also enter Rage Mode, which lets them unleash a powerful ability that comes with an impressive visual flourish. Power-ups litter the arenas, sometimes dropped by the Vortaak’s 1950s-style UFOs. These will either top up health and special meters, or send in Mothra for an aerial bombardment. When in doubt, you can always pick up a building and throw it at your opponent.

Each monster gets its own distinct moveset, and the uniformity of the controls means it's easy to try out everyone before you settle on a main character. Godzilla is a good all-rounder, and his Millennium model is the best-looking in the game. Gigan has a powerful teleport ability that can easily bamboozle an opponent. Several monsters can fly, with Mecha-King Ghidorah in particular being a formidable combo of offence and evasion.

There are some duds, like Megalon and Orga, who have utility but just don't feel great to play. I had the most fun with Mechagodzilla (here depicted in his Heisei Kiryu form for the remaster), who combines his Maser Cannon projectile with shoulder-mounted missile salvos.

Single-player offerings include the story-driven Adventure mode, which comes in three tiers of difficulty. Survival mode has you run a gauntlet and try to last as long as possible. For pure brainless wish fulfilment, there's Destruction mode, in which one or more kaiju lay waste to a city to rack up points.

There's also a full suite of local and online multiplayer modes, including a tournament ladder to decide once and for all who gets to be crowned king of the monsters. Monsters level up in the Adventure Mode, increasing base stats and adding abilities to their repertoire, which incentivises spending time with each fighter.

The system for unlocking new arenas and monsters, which involves repeating fights in the local modes, has been updated for this remaster. Previously, the ‘research’ tied to specific unlocks was fixed. Now you can freely choose which one you want to prioritise (pro tip: unlock Ghidorah first).

That said, there isn't much to do beyond the final bit of research, and getting 100% is a patience-testing loop of the same old fights. The magic of this game is in the pick-up-and-play nature of those battles, and it doesn't stand up to laborious repetition just to view some nice artwork.

The presentation of this remaster on Switch 2 is exemplary. Monster models and arenas have all been updated, and battles play out butter-smooth both docked and undocked. Undocked in particular looks great, with those big chunky fighters and diorama cityscapes really suited to portable play. There's a real fluidity to some of the action, particularly when monsters like Gigan close the distance with incredible speed.

The audio combines lovingly polished sound effects from the movies with a cacophony of city-levelling bangs and garbled military transmissions. It's a real shame there isn't Japanese vocal audio; the early-2000s English voices really take a layer of authenticity away.

Special mention must go to Director mode, an enhanced photo mode that lets you control the camera during a fight. Adjusting the speed and setting up the perfect shot of your favourite beasts laying into each other is addictive fun. You can see why Ishiro Honda made so many of these movies.

Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed…

#4254. Grand Theft Auto VI: New Original Song 'Pusher' Out Now, Full Score Album Arrives This December

Rockstar Games has released a new original song in Grand Theft Auto VI called "Pusher" by the game's composer duo, Justice. #4253. Grant Kirkhope Rayman Legends Retold - The Big Interview

Sam Woods is TheGamer’s Senior Reporter. He’s been in games journalism since 2020 and has undertaken a variety of roles in that time. These have included roles such as SEO Editor, Managing Editor at DualShockers, and Global Head of Gaming, and he's also been seen on the BBC. He was promoted to the Senior Reporter position in 2025 following a series of high-quality reports and exclusives for TheGamer.

Since 2020, Sam has written over 3,000 articles and specializes in telling the stories of the people behind the games. He’s interviewed the biggest game directors, some of the industry’s top talents, told the stories of how indie games came to be, and spoken to players about what really makes them tick. He’s also interviewed some of the world’s biggest musical artists to find out how the medium has inspired their work, and TV and Film actors about their roles in video game adaptations. He even hosted a PAX panel in 2021 and made a documentary in 2024 surrounding the creation of a Disney game.

Alongside this, Sam focuses on breaking news. He got the scoop on Perfect Dark’s cancellation, provided context on some AI drama, and revealed that Lady Dimitrescu’s actress would love to step back into the character’s giant shoes. These articles have been picked up by the biggest gaming sites, including IGN, GameSpot, and PC Gamer. He also loves to dive into the numbers behind the games.

Sam’s journey in games journalism has taken him all over the world. He’s covered Gamescom in Germany, Summer Game Fest in Los Angeles, and Tokyo Game Show in Japan, each on three occasions.

He’s been learning Japanese since 2024 with the intention of identifying and translating Japanese-language news and bringing it to English-language audiences first, something he’s done countless times.

Sam’s first review was 2020’s Battletoads reboot, and he’s since reviewed games in The Legend of Zelda, Super Mario, and Pokemon franchises.

There aren’t many composers in the video game space as esteemed as Grant Kirkhope. He’s won an Ivor Novello Award, and chances are he's composed music for at least one game you’ve played.

Starting at Rare in the mid-90s, his credits include series like Donkey Kong, Viva Piñata, Banjo-Kazooie, Minecraft Dungeons, Street Fighter, World of Warcraft, and Mario + Rabbids.

His latest adventure comes on Rayman Legends Retold, where he is composing for the game’s new world, The Land of the Livid Dead. Ahead of its release next month, we sat down with Kirkhope to discuss working on Rayman, his unique sound, and his illustrious career.

Kirkhope’s music traditionally has a lot of signature tells. He often combines woodwinds, strings, and xylophones to create whimsical soundtracks. Like Kirkhope, Rayman has sounds that are synonymous with the character. Did this process, merging two unique sounds, present a challenge?

“I guess because me and Christopher Héral worked together on the Mario Rabid Sparks of Hope Rayman DLC, we had an understanding. And so I think Ubisoft kind of spotted that our music kind of matched... We both write that kind of quirky music in a different way, and it kind of meets in the middle somewhere,” he tells me.

What about the character, is Rayman somebody that Kirkhope enjoys working with, given it's his second spell with the Ubisoft mascot after the Mario + Rabbids Sparks of Hope: Rayman in the Phantom Show DLC?

“It’s fantastic. Back in the day when I was at Rare, we were looking at Ubisoft; we were looking at them going, ‘Rayman's good’, and they were going, ‘Banjo is good.’ We always kept an eye on Rayman because he's a super cool character. He's Ubisoft's mascot, right,” he says. “He's a fantastic character. I feel like as a Brit, we like that kind of fart humor. I feel like it's built into British culture, right? So to get to work on that kind of character is great for British people because it's right up our street.”

While many games Kirkhope has composed for have featured spooky levels - think Banjo-Kazooie’s Mad Monster Mansion and Donkey Kong 64’s Creepy Castle - Land of the Livid Dead required the musician to take things up a notch.

“When I first started on it, I was expecting it to be that kind of traditional Rayman, quirky, irreverent, farts and all that stuff that goes on in Rayman, which is really cool. Right up my street, that is. But it wasn't. I got given the Land of the Livid Dead, which is really dark,” he says. “When I submitted ideas, they kept saying, ‘no darker, no darker, darker.’ I had to write quite dark music. They described it as ‘Rayman's no longer a kid. He's more of a teenager now. He's kind of a bit more mature.’ So I was like, ‘Oh.’ It was good fun to do. Because I like writing kind of spooky music with a bit of a quirk in it. I guess a bit Danny Elfman-y, probably.”

With the soundtrack being so dark, I began to worry it would lose some of Kirkhope’s trademark whimsy. I needn’t.

“I feel like it's got darkness in it, but there's still a little bit of humor. Because I think you can't do Rayman with that little bit of a nod and a wink, you know. And I feel like it's always got a bit of that. So it is dark. But it's still got a little bit of something in it just to maybe put a smile on your face, or maybe not scare you too much,” he grins.

I could be there. I could do that. Get me my bagpipes.

Over the last few years, Kirkhope has built a strong relationship with Ubisoft. His work on the Mario + Rabbids series was fantastic, and clearly it was good enough for them to call him back. I had to ask if Rayman was the only property he was working on, or whether, maybe, just maybe, this was a precursor to the troubled Beyond Good and Evil 2.

“No,” he says, chuckling. “It looks absolutely giant. I've got to say, when they showed it at E3, I thought it looked super cool. I'd work on anything for Ubisoft. I really would, because I've always had a good time with them.”

I decided to put that to the test. Would Grant Kirkhope work on an Assassin’s Creed game, and if so, when in the world would he choose?

“I'd love to have a crack at that, I've got to say. That would be a really cool project to work on, because it's such a cool game. And it's been through so many iterations of different scenarios,” he says. “London, Japan, the big massive Viking one. I’d love to do it. I think it’s unlikely, but I’d love to.

“Since I’m Scottish, it would have to be the whole Scotland-against-England thing. Back in the Middle Ages. William Wallace. Robert the Bruce. I could be there. I could do that. Get me my bagpipes.”

My chat with Kirkhope was brief. I only had 15 minutes with him, and despite Ubisoft having representatives on our call, I had to ask about some of his other work in quickfire fashion while I had the chance.

Firstly, I needed to know whether he thought the DK Rap, a song he created and has so often called “the worst piece of rap music ever,” would fly today.

“I feel like it's definitely a moment in time. I think at the time, the little kids got the joke, but the kind of cool teenagers are like, ‘this is the worst rap track in the history of rap tracks,’ and that’s because it is,” he says. “I feel like it's in the bracket of being so dreadfully bad that people love it and have a laugh with it. I feel like it's worked out in the end. I've had to wait, like, 25 years, but it got there in the end.”

What about the Goldeneye pause music? A viral TikTok video brought that back to the spotlight in the last few years.

“I claimed my TikTok artist profile. That song has 115 million plays. I have to watch that video every time it comes on my feed because he did such a good job. It’s fantastic, isn’t it?” Kirkhope says, smiling.

“I feel like I write these great, complex, orchestral pieces of music, and I'm proud of myself. And everyone's like, ‘yeah, but the DK rap, man, you know?’ Honestly, there are plenty of composers that never get known for anything. So if I'm known for the DK rap and the Golden Eye watch pause music, I'll take it any day. I feel like being known for anything is super humbling and just amazing that anybody gives a shit, right? So, yeah, I'll take it any day.”

Finally, with Donkey Kong rumored to be next in line for the Nintendo movie treatment, I had to ask Kirkhope how much he’d want to compose for it.

“Oh man, absolutely. Right now, this second, I’d drop everything to do that,” he says. “Even better, I’d do it with Dave [David Wise, composer on Donkey Kong Country, Donkey Kong Land, and Super Smash Bros. Melee, among others],” he tells me. “You can't do DK without Dave Wise's da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da, that tune [Donkey Kong Country’s Jungle Groove], and the DK rap. You've got to have those two.”

#4250. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it launched on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was announced back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly showed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

The game peaked at a decent 28,815 concurrent players (via SteamDB) on Steam one day after it launched, and considering how sticky it has been with the majority of those players so far - and the fact the launch itself was a surprise - there’s every chance those figures will improve over the course of this week as it picks up momentum.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating currently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.

You’re still need either a Google, Facebook, or Apple account to log into the game, same as you would on mobile. The Steam version does support cross-play with other platforms, so you’ll be able to play with your friends on mobile.

Ubisoft has released a fall update on the Assassin’s Creed franchise, providing news big and small on its flagship series. The news includes updates for existing games and smaller but significant insights on the various upcoming Assassin’s Creed games previously announced.

In terms of current games, Assassin’s Creed Valhalla is getting a long-requested New Game Plus thanks to a new update coming on November 5. This means you can start a fresh game while bringing over your progression items/level from your previous playthrough. This update will also introduce the following features:

This news comes a few days after New Game Plus arrived in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced.

Codname Invictis, a PvP multiplayer game, remains in development as Ubisoft shares it has incorporated feedback from players who, according to Ubisoft, “saw great potential in the foundations but wanted more of the pillars that define Assassin's Creed.” To this end, Ubisoft has spent months reworking Invictis to reflect this vague feedback and say the game is “now evolving in an exciting direction that better reflects those pillars while staying true to its multiplayer ambitions.”

As for the next single-player Assassin’s Creed, Codename Hexe, Ubisoft says it will share the next major update on this game in 2027. First announced in 2022, Codename Hexe is set during the 17th-century reign of the Holy Roman Empire, and the era's witch hunts will play a significant role.

With the release of Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced earlier this year, Ubisoft has given fans what they'll likely see as a disappointing update on potential future remakes: “One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin's Creed remake actively in development. #4247. Aonuma Calls the Water Temple His 'Overdue Homework' for Ocarina of Time Remake

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

With the release of the full remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2 later this week, old-school fans have been once again reminiscing on their many fond and not-so-fond memories from the N64 original. Whenever the topic of Ocarina of Time comes up, it’s often a safe bet that, sooner or later, things will turn to the infamous Water Temple, one of the elemental-themed dungeons in the game’s back half.

The Water Temple has long held a reputation for being one of the most legendarily frustrating dungeons in the Zelda franchise. Admittedly, a lot of the discourse is hyperbolic, based on memories of collective childhood, but the dungeon also definitely had some irritating quirks, from its confusing layout to the way it forced you to use your items and menus. If you didn’t have the little jingle that played every time you opened the pause menu permanently seared into your head before that dungeon, you sure did afterward.

The first gameplay trailer for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has confirmed that it has added a beloved feature from the 3DS version.

The designers of the Ocarina of Time remake are very aware of the long-standing vibe toward the Water Temple, as they discussed in an Ask the Developer feature on Nintendo’s official blog. Eiji Aonuma, the director and dungeon designer of the original game, now a senior officer and producer on the remake, spoke on how he created the original dungeon and how his perspective has changed since, with the remake’s director, Hokwai Ng, discussing how they’re making improvements without changing the fundamental vibe of the dungeon.

As part of the interview, Aonuma, Ng, and other members of the development team were asked how they approached the development of dungeons in the Ocarina of Time remake, particularly in relation to the original.

With a laugh, Aonuma said, “I had some overdue homework: I wanted to do something about the Water Temple I created 28 years ago.” He said that, back in the days of the N64, there were very few games that allowed you to do much of anything in an underwater setting. Therefore, if he was going to make an underwater dungeon, he wanted it to be distinct, something that brings across what could make being in such an environment fun. Aonuma is actually a hobbyist freediver, so he’s very acquainted with the distinct sensations of being completely underwater.

If he was going to make an underwater dungeon, he wanted it to be distinct, something that brings across what could make being in such an environment fun.

However, he concedes that the biggest problem with the Water Temple was one of navigation. “With the dungeon’s complex structure and a lot of item toggling involved, you often had to open the menu screen repeatedly, making it hard to keep track of where you were and which way you were facing.”

A look at the Water Temple from The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and how it should be remade with the same design.

Aonuma explained that, given the infamy that the Water Temple has accrued due to its difficulty, he had the dev team make some adjustments, not necessarily to make it flat-out easier, but to make it more playable and user-friendly.

Ng chimed in here to explain the team’s perspective, noting that most of the dungeon’s basic mechanisms have been preserved, but the layout has been slightly shifted in places to improve the overall signposting and flow of the dungeon. Additionally, some of the walls of the temple have been changed to a distinct lattice pattern, allowing you to see bits of the temple beyond the current room and get a better idea of where you are in relation to everything else, which will hopefully keep players from getting lost. Finally, item toggling has been streamlined, so you don’t need to keep opening the menu to equip and unequip your Iron Boots.

Are you excited for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake? So are we! Here are 8 changes we would like to see implemented in the remake.

At the end of the interview, Ng added that he hopes the slight differences between the remake and the original will spark some inter-generational conversation. He imagined a father playing the game with his child and saying, “You know, your Dad got stuck in the Water Temple plenty of times back in the day.”

Aonuma laughed and responded, “Then kids playing this version might say, “Come on, it’s not that hard.” Poor old Dad might end up feeling deflated.”

#4246. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4245. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Switch 2 Development Team Has Been Revealed

Nintendo has just released the first two parts of a new Ask the Developer series all about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2. Alongside a bunch of interesting insights about the game's development, the interview also finally reveals the development team behind it.

As it turns out, the Switch 2 remake was developed internally by Nintendo's Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) Production Group No. 3 — the team that has handled just about every Zelda entry since the early 2000s.

The remake saw HokWai Ng take on the role of Director (his first Dir. role at the company, though he also worked on Tears of the Kingdom), with Aya Shida (Pikmin 3, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, Tears of the Kingdom) on Art Direction, Hiroki Taguchi (Breath of the Wild) as the Program Director, and Masato Ohashi (Animal Crossing: New Horizons, Splatoon 3 Expansion Pass) as Music Lead and one of the Sound Directors.

There was a part of us that thought Nintendo might bring in another studio to work on the remake — particularly as it increasingly appeared more and more faithful to the original — but it's nice to see that it was an inside job instead. Worry not, Zelda legends Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi both served as producers on the project.

Parts three and four of the OoT Ask the Developer series will be released tomorrow (3rd November), so we're sure that there are even more dev stories to come. Gosh, what a week to be a Zelda fan!

#4244. Xbox Sweepstakes Can Let You Win a One-of-One X-Bite Alligator Console

Xbox is no stranger to strange marketing stunts over the years, but the gaming giant's latest promotion featuring the Xbox Series X is definitely one of the most unique we've ever seen. Initially announced on the official XboxWire account on X, the "Xbox Series X-Bite" itself is an incredibly detailed replica of an alligator that has swallowed a Series X, with the power button poking out of its back.

Although Xbox didn't specify what the promotion was explicitly for, it was heavily implied to be a tie-in advertisement for Grand Theft Auto 6 releasing later this month. While you won't be able to buy the leathery one-of-one console for yourself, Xbox shared that the X-Bite system would be given away entirely for free as a part of their newest sweepstakes.

While the quality of the alligator itself looks incredibly lifelike in photos, no animals were harmed in the making of the massive console measuring over five feet in length, as it was 3D modeled and sculpted by creature designer John Nolan Studio, who has worked on animatronics and other models for The Witcher, Jurassic World Dominion, and more.

If you're interested and have the space for the one-of-a-kind console yourself, all you have to do is follow Xbox on any of its social media accounts and repost their related sweepstakes announcement with #XbiteSweepstakes to enter for a chance to win. Ending on 11:59 PM PST on November 10th, the winner will have 48 hours to claim their reward before it goes to the next person.

The X-Bite giveaway is only available for US residents and those using public accounts, with the specific rules found on the Xbox Promotions website.

Even without explicitly naming Grand Theft Auto 6 in their advertisements, the details like "Xbox is heading to Florida," which has "stories you have to see to believe," and ensuring fans the system and custom bite-marked controller are "ready to play some of the biggest games of the year" are just about as clear a nod as you can get, especially when combined with the synth soundtrack playing in the background of the trailer.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4243. Sir Patrick Stewart, Star Trek, X-Men, And Myriad Video Games Actor, Passes Away

According to a report from The Hollywood Reporter, actor Sir Patrick Stewart has passed away at the age of 86. Stewart spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, shared that he died after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.”

Stewart was best known for his roles as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation (and its various spinoffs) and Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, but he did plenty of video game performing, too. Stewart played Emperor Uriel Septim VII in The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, one of the first characters you meet in the game, and Zobek in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow. He also played Jean-Luc Picard in about 10 different Star Trek games and Charles Xavier in five different X-Men games.

Stewart will always be a crucial voice and face in the legacy of sci-fi entertainment. Jean-Luc Picard will undoubtedly be an enduring and important character in the Star Trek franchise, and that's thanks to Stewart's portrayal of the starship captain. His portrayal of Charles Xavier also helped to legitimize the comic book movie, and he will appear again as the character in this year's upcoming Avengers: Doomsday.

Our thoughts are with his friends and family, and the millions of fans (of which I include myself) who are mourning his loss. Let's all drink some Earl Grey tea in his honor today.

#4242. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

#4241. Nioh 3’s generous demo is out now, and your progress carries over to the full game

If you’re looking for a way to check out one of the biggest releases of early 2026, Team Ninja has made it easy for you.

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically launched first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

The Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another big reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

The demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

#4240. 10 Action-Adventure Games That Are Unexpected Masterpieces

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

The action-adventure genre is one of the broadest in the entire video game industry, encompassing countless experiences ranging from stealth and hack-and-slash to horror and beat 'em ups.

Thanks to this broad definition, countless masterpieces fall under its umbrella, including many that, unfortunately, haven't achieved the popularity they deserve due to fierce competition.

Even within the realm of major blockbusters, not all underrated titles are obscure indie games—there are games that have fallen just short of mainstream success, though I'm here to help rectify that.

So, in order to shed light on some lesser-known campaigns that haven't yet cemented their undeniable excellence in the collective consciousness, I invite you to explore this list of ten action-adventure games that are unexpected masterpieces.

As the least recognized work from Tango Gameworks, a studio that has certainly gifted us with numerous magnificent journeys, Ghostwire: Tokyo stands out among the games with the greatest disparity between its quality and its fame.

Boasting one of the finest atmospheres crafted this decade, wandering the streets of Shibuya, soaring across rooftops, and taking down the most terrifying yokai imaginable is, by far, one of my highlights of the decade.

Whether in stealth or direct magical combat, tackling one of its turbulent side quests or hunting for collectibles, the game strikes an outstanding balance between making each mechanic satisfying while still maintaining a constant sense of terror in its setting.

As far as first-person games go, Ghostwire: Tokyo is part of the most immersive, rewarding, and distinctive I've played this generation, which is saying something considering the titans with which it shares category.

As the years have gone by, games that adhere to the Metroidvania philosophy have become one of my greatest obsessions, which inevitably led me to fall in love with Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo.

Its ability to capture the nostalgia of the Game Boy Advance era while boasting the refined design and execution of modern products demonstrates its creators' immeasurable talent, who also imbued it with an impressive thematic personality.

The critiques of various strategic production industries resonate with our current times, while in the process, the game leverages the yoyo as a central gameplay element to make traversal, combat, exploration, and customization an absolute delight that's also pretty unique.

Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo is among the finest indie titles I've enjoyed in the last couple of years, and anything other than recognizing it as brilliant is to underestimate its potential.

If you're interested in unfairly criticized titles, I recommend checking out these ten underrated action-adventure games that were badly reviewed.

As someone who didn't experience the franchise's heyday, Shinobi: Art of Vengeance not only caught me completely off guard, but I can think of very few resurrections that have felt so powerful.

The absolute masterwork of action and platforming that this title is results in frankly mind-blowing sequences, flowing seamlessly between both dimensions to deliver a thrilling adventure that doesn't let you breathe for a second.

As you unlock combos, powers, and movement abilities, you encounter an ever-increasing series of challenges that push the game's mechanics to their limits, which are meticulously refined to ensure you have complete control over every pixel.

Few titles in 2025 felt as satisfying to complete 100%, so Shinobi: Art of Vengeance stands as a masterfully unexpected example that, when you don't know what to do with your old IPs, outsourcing to an indie studio to work on them is the best possible idea.

The Legend of Zelda's heirs number in the hundreds of thousands, but that didn't stop Death's Door from emerging as one of its most intelligent and charismatic great-great-grandchildren.

The game perfectly understands the enjoyment that lies in discovery and exploration through iteration, inviting us on a diverse adventure with plenty of colorful biomes, enemies, characters, and circumstances that evoke all kinds of emotions.

Curiosity, fear, happiness, sadness, worry... The title silently manages a multitude of emotions both thematically and in its gameplay, limiting progression to allow for exploration of its expansive world at a prodigious pace.

When discussing isometric titles that combine action, platforming, and puzzles in the best possible way, Death's Door is at the description's forefront, though it's the ease and finesse with which it achieves this that's truly unexpected.

Castlevania is a series that went through some difficult years after the turn of the century, and it wasn't until Castlevania: Lords of Shadow arrived that the IP unexpectedly found some relief amidst so many setbacks, astonishingly becoming the best-selling game in the entire IP.

MercurySteam crafted one of the most beautiful and satisfying hack-and-slash games in the genre's history, finally adapting the saga's formula perfectly to 3D without losing an ounce of its core identity.

The whip feels better than ever, as do the movement mechanics, the puzzles, and the progression systems, all enhanced in the best possible way thanks to a magnificently crafted story and characters that keep you on the edge of your seat until the very last second.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow completely forgoes being conceptually innovative, but the sacrifice, given it guaranteed us an extremely excellent title in all its facets, was totally worth it even when nobody was betting on such a resounding success.

If you enjoy discovering incredible titles without proper recognition, I recommend these ten best action-adventure games forgotten by time.

In the years when God of War slowed down, and Devil May Cry practically disappeared, a third icon emerged from absolutely nowhere to keep the hack-and-slash genre alive (with Bayonetta's permission): Darksiders.

Drawing inspiration from both Santa Monica Studio's work and The Legend of Zelda, Vigil Games crafted a splendidly elaborate tale and setting within Judeo-Christian mythology, one of the least explored in the video game industry.

Giant bosses based on satisfying gimmicks, varied and refreshing puzzles that make the most of War's arsenal and movement capabilities, phenomenal art design for both environments and enemies... It's the complete package.

That the company's first title would be such a presentation of knowledge in the genre's fundamentals was unforeseen even for the team itself, but much more for the hundreds of thousands who, like me, stumbled upon Darksiders by chance and have been hooked ever since.

Returning to the topic of franchises forced to reinvent themselves to adapt to modern times, not even the most optimistic projections for the Tomb Raider reboot could have predicted the absolute brilliance it would become.

Going back to Lara Croft's origins resulted in one of the quintessential action-adventure games of the entire generation, achieving an astonishing symphony of survival mechanics, realistic yet compelling gunplay, and simply fantastic settings and stories.

Each set piece surpasses the last, and the spectacular scenery contrasts perfectly with the brutal and tense story the legendary archaeologist faces, all while possessing the intriguing premise of not yet being the intrepid adventurer we all know, but rather a young, still-innocent graduate.

From concept to execution, Tomb Raider is a tapestry of sound decisions that, among other things, reminded Uncharted fans that Nathan Drake only managed to run because Lara Croft walked first.

I know that nowadays we're used to indie masterpieces being released every couple of months, but back in the day, before that was the norm, Hyper Light Drifter arrived like a hurricane of grandeur.

Taking Dark Souls' harshness, non-linearity, and disorientation, Heart Machine assembled an adventure that is both cryptic and captivating, where the gameplay and narrative direction are entirely in the player's hands.

Where to go and why are questions that only the user can answer through exploration, embarking on an intense and introspective journey where bosses and secrets abound, motivating us to explore every last corner of its silent world.

Along with gorgeous pixel art, a remarkable sound design, and a simple yet perfect gameplay loop, Hyper Light Drifter built a castle with just a few blocks, a feat reserved only for the greatest.

If you're looking for modern games to get lost in, I recommend the ten best adventure games of the 2020s (so far).

The reviews for Asura's Wrath were so scathing that it took me a decade to finally deign to play it, and the sheer shock of finishing it in tears when the credits rolled was beyond words.

Yes, every single one of the comments regarding its poor gameplay was, is, and will be correct, since it's a beat 'em up where the best parts of the gameplay are the on-rails shooting and quick-time events, and that doesn't exactly reflect well on a title of this genre.

Regardless, when you have such an incredible plot, abundant with charismatic characters, memorable scenes, robust mythology, and eccentrically immeasurable cinematics, I couldn't care less that every encounter boils down to mashing the attack button a hundred times a second.

The intercosmic scale that Asura's Wrath handles in its presentation and spectacle is monumental, unique, and emotional enough to overlook its mediocre mechanics, being the only case in the entire genre where it's a masterpiece even without being fun in the traditional sense.

Bucking the trend in the genre, whose disdain for stealth became evident in the last decade, Arkane Studios made a tremendous statement in 2012 with Dishonored's release.

Coming from another underrated gem, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, the studio embraced the lingering force of immersive sims and materialized it into a project that excels as both a stealth game and an action-adventure game.

Boasting some of the best level design in video game history, along with a story that evolves based on the player's actions rather than dialogue choices, Dishonored is one of the century's defining power fantasies.

Between Dunwall's perfect setting, the outstanding array of gadgets and powers that allow for creative and expansive use of stealth and violence, and the majestic musical pieces that accompany us, it's clear that the love for stealth games will never die as long as this IP remains available.

Years go by, and I still wonder if the genre has enough strength to produce a title that surpasses Dishonored, but for now, it remains on the throne without any concern about being replaced.

In this list, we'll discuss our picks for the best action-adventure games that go beyond a hundred hours, from RPGs to known open-world titles.

#4239. Death Stranding Isolations Animated Series Gets New Teaser Trailer

A new teaser trailer for Death Stranding Isolations, an upcoming animated series coming exclusively to Disney+ and Hulu next year, premiered during Kojima Productions’ 10th Anniversary Exhibition Beyond the Strand. The series was first announced last year.

Death Stranding Isolations tells an original story in the Death Stranding universe set immediately after the events of the first game. Isolations is created by Japanese animation studio E&H Production (Ninja Kamui, Bullet/Bullet, Magic Knight Rayerath) and directed by Takayuki Sano.  Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima serves as executive producer.

Today’s teaser video provides the following story synopsis:

The Death Stranding—a catastrophic series of explosions caused when the dead crept into our world and collided with the living.

In the wake of this cataclysm, many were forced to live in absolute isolation—among them, a young girl. Although this lonely existence was forced upon her, she soon grows to prefer solitude, eschewing all opportunities for real human connection and allowing herself to be strung along by fate.

In Death Stranding, legendary game creator Hideo Kojima brought you a haunting vision of a shattered world. Now, that world expands into new frontiers with a brand-new animation series.

Under the guidance of director Takayuki Sano, world-class hand-drawn animations have been brought to life by renowned studio “E&H production” (NINJA KAMUI, BULLET/BULLET, the Magic Knight Rayearth television series).

The story is set in North America immediately after Sam—the protagonist of the game—reconnects the continent by means of the Chiral Network. However, as America is reborn from the ashes, the renewed connections that bind it together bring about new and unforeseen consequences.

In this tumultuous new landscape, there are some who walk a different path to the one chosen by Sam and his Bridges comrades: a wise old man who connects people through a method that defies all reckoning; a female soldier ensnared in a cycle of war and destruction; a boy who seethes with rage at the absurdity of his life...and of course, the girl who chose to sever all ties with the outside world...Fate has other plans for her, however, and chance encounters see her launched headfirst into a world she does not recognize.

Death Stranding Isolations is coming to Disney+ and Hulu in 2027. It’s one of the three planned big-screen adaptations of the series. An animated movie called Death Stranding: Mosquito (working title) is also in the works alongside a live-action Death Stranding film by A24.

For more on Death Stranding, check out our reviews for the first game and its 2025 sequel. You can also read the latest update on Kojima Productions’ upcoming stealth-espionage game, Physint.

#4237. EA Reportedly Closed BioWare To Invest In Developing Star Wars Battlefront III Instead Of The Next Mass Effect

Electronic Arts shut down the legendary RPG studio BioWare last week, ending development on an untitled fifth Mass Effect game. Since then, we've seen what appears to be a leaked trailer for the game, which suggests it might have been called Mass Effect Universe, and heard a sneak peek at what Grammy-winning composer Austin Wintory was cooking up for the beloved sci-fi RPG series. Over the past week, fans across the internet have tried to piece together how a publisher could decide to shut down a studio as prolific as BioWare, but according to a new Bloomberg report, the answer is Star Wars.

More specifically, Bloomberg writes that, presented with the opportunity to develop Star Wars Battlefront III with Disney, the publisher, which went private last year after a $55 billion acquisition,  chose to invest its money into that instead of BioWare's in-development Mass Effect sequel. The publication writes that EA looked at its portfolio for the coming years and had two massive sci-fi investments it could continue: Star Wars Battlefront III or BioWare's next Mass Effect. Even though Mass Effect was well into development, and even though the Battlefront threequel hasn't even entered development, EA chose to continue with the latter. And so BioWare was shut down, and Mass Effect development ended, though Bloomberg's sources say there are other, less significant reasons the studio was shuttered, too.

Those other factors include the poor reception to 2017's Mass Effect: Andromeda, the failure of Anthem in 2019, and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which, despite garnering positive critical reception, apparently missed EA's sales expectations by 50%.

There's also the uncomfortable reality that BioWare made progressive LGBTQIA+ positive games but was a studio within a publisher house now partially owned by the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, a government fund from a country where same-sex activity, including marriage, is criminalized, sometimes punishable by death; these harsh laws extend to other facets of the LGBTQIA+ community. Another investment partner in this acquisition of EA is Affinity Partners, a Miami-based investment firm founded and run by former White House senior advisor Jared Kushner, who is the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, a political figure who imposes laws that discriminate against the LGBTQIA+ community, especially the 1% of Americans who are transgender; Trump has also been known to mock this community in various ways. No official statements say BioWare shut down because of its progressive leanings, but one has to wonder if that was a factor, especially after reports that BioWare scrubbed diversity from demos to avoid negative feedback from EA (thanks, Kotaku).

When BioWare closed last week, only 50 employees remained, all working on the next Mass Effect, after years of layoffs at the studio.

A Mass Effect TV series is still in the works at Amazon, even though EA seems to have hung up Commander Shepard's video game suit for good.

#4236. Where To Find Every Resource In Loftia

Tracking down crafting materials can be a little tedious in Loftia, especially when you're not entirely sure where to start looking. The map is split into four distinct areas, each with its own collection of useful resources to help you with your crafting and building projects.

From Glass Coils and Scrap Wire at the Solar Farm to Portobello Mushrooms, knowing where to look will save you plenty of wandering around. Some materials are simply lying on the ground, while others require a little extra work, like breaking microwaves with a hammer or washing machines to get what you need. Here's where to find every resource and what you'll need to collect them!

Below, we detail each resource/material and where to find it within Loftia City!

Head to the Solar Farm in the northwest corner of the map. Break microwaves with a hammer to collect Glass Coils.

Visit the Solar Farm in the northwest corner of the map. Scrap Wire can be found sitting on tables and scattered across the ground. You can also occasionally get some by breaking microwaves with a hammer.

Head to the Solar Farm in the northwest corner of the map. Tires are found outside, often near trees.

Travel to the Hills in the northeast corner of the map, just east of Pebble. Portobello Mushrooms are scattered throughout the grassy area, and you'll need shears to collect them.

Visit the Hills in the northeast corner of the map. You can find Plant Fiber throughout the area, particularly in tall grass and grass bundles.

Head to the Hills in the northeast corner of the map. Search the bushes throughout the area to find Wild Berries.

Travel to the Construction Site in the southeast corner of the map. Look for the small wooden boxes scattered throughout the area and break them to collect Scrap Wood.

Visit the Construction Site in the southeast corner of the map. Clay can be found in several spots scattered across the ground throughout the area.

Head to the Scrap Quarter in the southwest corner of the map, near Milo. Screws can be found scattered throughout the area.

Visit the Scrap Quarter in the southwest corner of the map, near Milo. Look for piles of debris containing bottles to find Plastic Discards.

Travel to the Scrap Quarter in the southwest corner of the map, near Milo. Break the washing machines scattered throughout the area to collect Metal

#4235. Nintendo Wanted To Remake Ocarina Of Time To "Trigger New Insights" For Future Titles

"Hang on, why is Nintendo remaking Ocarina of Time again?" It's a natural question that might have occurred to you in the last few months, and in the latest Ask the Developer interview, Series Producer Eiji Aonuma had the answer.

Part of the reason for returning to the title, it turns out, was to try to "trigger new insights" from the developers that may feed into future Zelda games. "Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles," Aonuma-san says. "That led me to wonder, 'Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?'"

"I started to wonder how they'd interpret The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games," he continues. "By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development."

While he describes the potential behind such insights as "extremely valuable," he also notes that it wasn't the only reason he wanted to return to OoT for the series' 40th anniversary. The game's structure is drastically different from more recent series entries like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, two games that a whole generation of Zelda fans will have grown up on (as sobering a thought as that is), so Nintendo wanted to showcase a different style of gameplay, too:

In The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, part of the fun comes from progressing through a carefully paced adventure and story, gradually building up the player’s growth and their understanding of the narrative along the way. We wanted players who had grown accustomed to Legend of Zelda games like Breath of the Wild, where they can freely choose their own path from the start, to experience that kind of gameplay as well

Whether revisiting Ocarina of Time actually does influence any future games' design decisions remains to be seen, but if you're looking for GoodGameTM inspiration, it certainly isn't a bad place to start.

The Ask the Developer interview also revealed that Ocarina of Time was internally developed at Nintendo, with HokWai Ng in the Director's seat.

#4234. Infinity Nikki ushers in the Year of the Horse with... a deer-themed Version 2.2

Chromatic Beings Everbright, the latest major Infinity Nikki update, has arrived, bringing Chinese New Year celebrations vibe to the game.

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, open-world dress-up RPG, has delivered yet another big content drop in the form of Chromatic Beings Everbright. The latest update brings the game up to version 2.2, and introduces a new narrative chapter, and gameplay taking place around a festival narrative.

If you couldn’t guess already, the new theme is Bloom Festival, inspired by Chinese New Year celebrations.

The big new story chapter takes place in the Infinity Nikki’s Wanxiang Realm. This deceptively serene and blissful region hides a dark secret, however. Chromafaces, the mythical inhabitants of the realm, have to embody fixed identities that dictate how they live and work.

These are doled out through Character Tokens, which are used to assign roles to each individual. The story follows Nikki as she uncovers the script that runs the realm and the facade it props up. Nikki will help free Chromafaces and dispel the illusion.

The Wanxiang Realm is split into three areas. Cai Ye is your typical lantern-lit district, where festivals and fireworks happen. Kongming Gorge is almost the opposite of that; a quiet and cold place. Finally, Jiuhua Pavilion literally floats above the region, and it's home to neverending music and dance.

The other big addition in 2.2 are the two new 5-Star Resonance Outfits with some interesting gameplay implications. Where Wanxiang Weaves Life is inspired by wuxia aesthetics, and true to its inspirations, it lets Nikki shapeshift into different Spirit Personas - and automatically collect resources in her vicinity.

Chroma's Mortal Heart, on the other hand, allows Nikki to fly around the Wanxiang Realm, drawing on the power of the Celestial Deer. This outfit also uses Celestial Deer Vision to automatically ping and mark treasure chests around her.

You can also look forward to Nefarious Shadows, a new Ability Outfit, which lets Nikki see through disguises, and reveals hidden paths in the world.

As with every major update, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.

If you’re jumping back into the game soon, be sure to hit up our Infinity Nikki codes page for some freebies.

#4233. The Top 10 Best Horror Games To Play This Halloween

Humans are drawn to horror in all forms, real life and fiction. Perhaps it’s the desire to get as close to death as possible without actually dying; perhaps it’s the morality of life and knowing death comes for all of us; perhaps all our heads are just a little miswired. Whatever the reason, we flock to movies where supernatural entities and puppets on tricycles upend otherwise lovely lives, TV shows where murderous cults kill and stump local detectives, and books where the words on the page seem to follow you to bed. Games, however, go a step further, letting you enter the horror and control it (or become its victim), and you could argue that, as a result, they’re the most immersive form of fiction.

We at Game Informer love a healthy dose of horror from time to time, and we often review games like this. Some terrify us. Others… don’t. And the best ones stick with us for years and years after the credits. Below is a list of 10 of the best horror games we’ve played recently. This isn’t an all-time list, so don’t fret if your personal favorite isn’t here. Instead, this is a collection of 10 horror games ordered by release date that we think are great for spooky season and beyond. Let us know in the comments what you would add to the list!

The cozy corner of the horror genre seems to have exploded overnight, and now tons of new slice-of-life horror games are in various stages of development. That said, the team behind newcomer The Village in the Shade is no stranger to the form; they made the Yomawari series, a cute-and-terrifying collection of creepy virtual tales. The Village in the Shade takes things back to the homestead, giving you (a child who emerged from a hole in the ground and was immediately given the responsibility of running an entire farm by yourself) the freedom to plant, sow, reap, ranch, and more. Just follow the important rules: don't go out at night, don't share secrets, and don't leave the village among others. You wouldn't want to break the rules, right? You could, theoretically, go about your idyllic rural living. But as you unravel the threads of what this village is, who you are, and why you're here, it's hard not to get drawn into the strange, mysterious, delightfully disturbing truths hiding in its shadows. Just don't forget to water your turnips before you go sneaking out again.

Fans of survival horror and old-school FMV adventure games will find plenty to love (and fear) in Tenebris Somnia. When a young woman visits her ex-boyfriend’s apartment and discovers he's trapped in a hellish dream world, it kicks off a well-executed survival-horror trek of inventive puzzles and resource management to overcome dangerous monsters. High-production, live-action cutscenes help tell the story of a deteriorating relationship and the toll an indie horror film took on its creators, and they play an important role in gameplay. Tenebris Somnia may not look like much due to its classic pixelated presentation, but its scares and story captivate. – Our Review

Resident Evil Requiem is not just one of the best Resident Evil games, but it’s also one of the best horror games ever made. It features a unique dual-protagonist structure. Grace Ashcroft is timid, new to the whole “shooting zombies in the head while dealing with Umbrella viruses” thing, and is generally just trying to do her job. Leon S. Kennedy, however, is a veteran of all that and more. Requiem splits its runtime between the two characters, letting you experience both sides of Capcom’s marquee survival-horror style. Grace’s sections leave your hands clammy and your blood pressure high as you desperately try to survive. Leon’s sections leave your hands shaking with adrenaline and your blood pumping with excitement as he mows down zombies (sometimes literally, courtesy of those pesky chainsaws). The result is a Resident Evil game that blends two typical RE experiences – terrifying and tough or exhilarating over-the-top action – into one cohesive package. It’s perfect for someone who wants to feel scared and then soon after receive the catharsis of being the one in control, like being the tragic victim who dies in Act One of the horror movie and the last one standing who lives to tell the tale. – Our Review

Little Nightmares developer Tarsier Studios has a knack for delivering creepy side-scrolling adventures, but Reanimal eschews any whimsy to become its scariest game yet. While mechanically it is similar to Little Nightmares and still puts small children in unimaginable peril, Reanimal is capital-H horror thanks largely to its terrifying threats and disturbing animal-themed imagery (this probably isn’t the game for animal lovers; some messed-up stuff happens to these critters). Escaping the game’s island setting is thrilling and chilling whether you’re playing alone or with a friend in co-op. Months after release, we’re still thinking about Reanimal’s memorable final sequence, which is worth the price of admission on its own. – Our Review

2001’s Silent Hill 2 is considered one of the best horror video games of all time for good reason. At release, it was a graphical powerhouse, using the PlayStation 2's horsepower to create a setting that begged to be explored, even though every bone in your body said you shouldn’t. The remake from developer Bloober Team took on a big task in modernizing the game without losing the original’s soul, and it did a great job. Among all the recent Silent Hill releases (Silent Hill f, Silent Hill: Townfall), the remake is our favorite. The story of James Sunderland and his troubling relationship with his departed wife is complex, emotional, and – important for the purposes of this list – unsettling and scary. – Our Review

Alan Wake 2 is an excellent pick for some spooky madness, in the vein of David Lynch’s seminal Twin Peaks mystery-surrealist series. Don’t worry too much about the “2” part of the game’s title. You just need to know that the titular Alan Wake character is a not-great writer who acts like he’s really great, his wife is missing, and he got trapped in the ambiguous Dark Place. He’s only one half of the Alan Wake 2 equation, with his segments set in a dream-like version of New York City. Playing as him feels the most Twin Peaks-y. The other half is Saga, a police officer who arrives in the Pacific Northwest town of Bright Falls to investigate a murder that might be linked to a cult. You can expect more traditional survival-horror gameplay from her. But this is still a Remedy Entertainment game, and without spoiling anything, it goes places. And along the way, you can expect plenty of scares. Turn the lights down low (or off), light a candle, and sit back and enjoy one of Remedy’s best games. – Our Review

Square Enix has gone two-for-two with its Paranormasight series, an anthology of stories about the strange and occult. And while the more recent Mermaid's Curse is a brilliant tale all its own, the first entry – The Seven Mysteries of Honjo – brings significantly more scares. A group of people in the city of Honjo find themselves caught in a spectral battle royale, using powerful objects and conditions to curse one another, with the allure of a prize at the end. Its magic isn't just in the flowchart timeline, where you can hop between different perspectives and protagonists to see how events play out from every angle, but also in the gorgeous stereoscopic environments and narrative puzzles. Adventure games are a classic genre, and Paranormasight will remind you of what the genre is capable of the moment you slowly spin your camera around, your eyes peeking out from behind your fingers.

Survival horror can contain multitudes, and as the years have worn on, the genre has grown to encompass a wide range of action-combat mechanics. Signalis feels like a re-centering in that respect. It's an isometric survival-horror indie project from developer rose-engine, filled with clever puzzles, scarce resources, limited inventory slots, and looming, oppressive dread. As the Replika unit Elster, you delve deep into a remote complex filled with horrors and monsters, searching for something, or someone, waiting down below. While love for classic horror games and other hallmarks of genre fiction will certainly draw you in, the stylish presentation and devastatingly human core will keep you forging ahead to the finale. Once you've breached the surface of Signalis' retro-future super-structures, you won't be able to turn back.

In horror movies, audiences often groan at a protagonist for putting themselves in seemingly grave danger just to learn more about a cursed amulet or bloodthirsty killer. But in Immortality, you are the protagonist, and despite a lingering sense that you shouldn't be digging into the archives of these abandoned films, each eerie new scene makes you want to dive deeper. It's a game about Marisa Marcel, an actress who almost starred in three movies in the late 20th century, but has since disappeared. None of the movies were ever released due to mysterious circumstances, but you have access to the archived, unedited live-action footage, including behind-the-scenes conversations. By scrubbing through footage, you can select people or items in each scene and jump to random footage from any other movie that includes the same person or item. The approach to puzzle-solving is unique and keeps you appropriately disoriented. The mystery at the center is an unsettling treat to unravel, and scary in new and unexpected ways. Immortality is one of a kind and an easy recommendation for horror fans who want to try something a little different.

In the decade since launch, Dead by Daylight has continued to succeed, thanks to a dedicated (and newcomer-friendly) fanbase and its towering roster of original and licensed personas from across pop culture horror. The asymmetrical multiplayer title has become an anthology of horror’s biggest faces, including Freddy Krueger, Ghostface, Pyramid Head, and even the Xenomorph. Whether you play as a Survivor, trying to escape all manner of nightmare locations through stealth and cunning, or as a Killer, whose experience feels more like a hunting club, you’ll understand why Dead by Daylight has become a recurring destination for fans of the gruesome and bizarre.

Read about the making of Dead by Daylight and how it sunk its teeth into millions of players in our six-page exclusive feature in Issue 368 (p. 42), available in our magazine archive to anyone with a free Game Informer account.
